model_answer: Antarctica is pristine, never settled by humans, so it preserves the planet's history: the story of Gondwana and continental drift, and ice-cores holding half a million years of carbon records. label: PYQ-style
stem: 'Take care of the small things and the big things will fall into place.' Explain with reference to phytoplankton. (40–50 words)
hint: Grasses of the sea; photosynthesis; food chain; ozone depletion; carbon cycle.
model_answer: Phytoplankton are tiny single-celled plants, the grasses of the sea, which feed the whole marine food chain through photosynthesis and absorb carbon dioxide. Ozone depletion lets in ultraviolet light that harms them, and any damage would ripple up to fish, seals and whales and upset the carbon cycle. Protecting the smallest organisms protects the whole system.

label: PYQ-style
stem: What lessons about the Earth's past, present and future does Tishani Doshi draw from her journey to Antarctica? (120–150 words)
hint: Journey → Gondwana and records → human impact in 12,000 years → phytoplankton/ozone → Students on Ice → walk and question.
model_answer:
Tishani Doshi's hundred-hour journey from Madras to Antarctica aboard the Akademik Shokalskiy becomes a lesson in time. The white continent tells the past: 650 million years ago it lay at the heart of Gondwana, joined to India, and its rocks and ice-cores still hold the record of continental drift and half a million years of climate.

Against that span, human civilisation is only 12,000 years old, yet in that blink we have burned fossil fuels and wrapped the planet in a carbon-dioxide blanket. Antarctica shows the present consequences first — retreating glaciers, collapsing ice shelves — and raises the question whether the West Antarctic ice sheet will melt and disrupt the Gulf Stream. The threat to phytoplankton from ozone loss teaches that the smallest things uphold the largest systems.

For the future, Doshi points to Geoff Green's Students on Ice: young people who see the ice become the policy-makers who will protect it. Walking on a metre of ice over the ocean, she wonders whether Antarctica will one day be warm — the question we must answer.

scheme.step: The journey and the past: Gondwana, ice-core records
The present: human impact in 12,000 years; phytoplankton and ozone
The future: melting, Students on Ice, youth as policy-makers
Conclusion with the closing question; expression and length

label: PYQ-style
stem: How has the human race, in a very short time, put the planet at risk? How does Antarctica make this visible, and what does the author suggest as a way forward? (120–150 words)
hint: 12,000 years vs geological time → wars, cities, resources, fossil fuels, carbon blanket → ice sheets, Gulf Stream, ozone, phytoplankton → education of the young → humility.
model_answer:
Set against the Earth's history, humans are newcomers: civilisation is about 12,000 years old, a few seconds on the geological clock. Yet in that time we have multiplied, built cities, fought wars and battled other species for limited resources. By burning fossil fuels we have wrapped the planet in a blanket of carbon dioxide and pushed up its temperature.

Antarctica makes the danger visible. Its ice sheets hold most of the world's fresh water, and glaciers there are already retreating and ice shelves collapsing. If the West Antarctic ice sheet melts, sea levels and the Gulf Stream could change for the whole world. Ozone depletion over the Southern Ocean threatens the phytoplankton on which every marine creature depends.

Doshi's way forward is education and humility. Geoff Green's Students on Ice takes future policy-makers to see the ice for themselves, because seeing moves people to act. And her closing thought — will Antarctica one day be warm? — asks each of us to take care of the small things before the big ones fail.

scheme.step: Human time vs geological time; human activities and the carbon blanket
Antarctica's evidence: glaciers, ice sheets, Gulf Stream, ozone and phytoplankton
Way forward: Students on Ice, small things, humility
